summary: Describes a mechanism to reduce redundant packet transmissions in the IS-IS routing protocol, as described in ISO 10589, for richly connected networks.

plainLanguage.summary: If routers are all connected to each other, they repeat the same news many times. This lets them stay quiet where it is not needed.

subtitle: Reducing redundant packet flooding in mesh network topologies

tldr.problem: In networks where routers are connected in a full mesh (every router directly connected to every other router), the IS-IS routing protocol floods link state packets redundantly, with each router retransmitting the same packet to all neighbors, wasting bandwidth and processing.
tldr.mechanism: Mesh groups mark circuits as meshSet, meshBlocked, or meshInactive, and modify the flooding rules so that a packet received on one mesh circuit is not re-sent on other circuits in the same mesh group, since all mesh members already have a direct connection.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism is deployed in production networks to reduce flooding overhead in mesh topologies while remaining backwards compatible with implementations that do not support it.

facts.label: Redundant transmissions in full mesh
facts.value: N-2 extra copies per LSP in a mesh of N routers

today: RFC 2973 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. The mesh group optimization mechanism it describes is deployed in production IS-IS networks.

sections.title: Mesh Flooding Problem
sections.content:
The Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) routing protocol floods Link State PDUs (LSPs) through networks to keep all routers synchronized on topology information. In ATM or frame relay networks, a full mesh topology occurs when routers connect to each other via point-to-point virtual circuits with every pair of routers having a direct link.

The standard IS-IS flooding rule is simple: when a router receives a new LSP, it stores it and retransmits it out all circuits except the source circuit. In a full mesh of N routers, this creates N-2 redundant transmissions of each LSP: if System 1 sends an LSP to all neighbors, and System 2 receives it, System 2 will retransmit it to Systems 3 and 4 even though they already have direct connections to System 1 and will receive the LSP directly from the source.

In a network with many routers connected in a mesh, this redundancy wastes both bandwidth and CPU processing effort with little benefit to reliability, since the mesh provides full connectivity and direct paths already.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if every time one person learned a piece of news, they told everyone else, and then everyone they told also told everyone else. That works, but it's inefficient. In a group where everyone already talks to everyone else, the news spreads fast without all the repeated telling.

sections.title: Mesh Group Definition and Marking
sections.content:
The RFC defines a mesh group as a set of point-to-point circuits providing full connectivity to a set of routers. Each circuit is assigned a state (meshInactive, meshBlocked, or meshSet) and, if state is meshSet, an integer mesh group number.

The key modification to IS-IS is in the flooding rule: when a router receives an LSP on a circuit in meshSet state, it does NOT retransmit the LSP back out other circuits in the same mesh group. This is because all routers in a mesh group are directly connected to each other, so they will receive the LSP directly from the source. Circuits in meshBlocked state do not send or receive LSPs at all; circuits in meshInactive state follow the standard flooding rule.

The RFC also modifies how Complete Sequence Number PDUs (CSNPs, which synchronize the database between neighbors) are handled. On circuits marked meshSet or meshBlocked, CSNPs are sent periodically for synchronization. On meshInactive circuits, CSNPs are sent only once during initialization.
sections.plainLanguage: Circuits between routers are marked as 'mesh' (in the same fully-connected group), 'blocked' (not part of the mesh), or 'normal' (regular circuit). When a mesh circuit receives the news, it doesn't pass it along to other mesh circuits because they already heard it directly.

sections.title: Interoperation and Limitations
sections.content:
Mesh groups are backwards compatible: a router that does not implement mesh groups will not receive different packets. It will see extra Complete Sequence Number PDUs on some circuits (because mesh-enabled routers send CSNPs more frequently) but will respond correctly to them. This allows gradual deployment.

However, the RFC documents significant drawbacks. Mesh groups rely on correct manual configuration by operators. If configuration errors combined with link failures create a partitioned flooding topology, LSPs may not propagate in a timely fashion, potentially causing routing loops or black holes. The document notes that numbered mesh groups suffer from brittleness: losing a transit link between mesh groups can partition the flooding topology unpredictably.

The authors state that in practice, administrators do not deploy numbered mesh groups at scale. Instead, they configure circuits as meshBlocked to prune flooding (a technique termed 'poor man's mesh groups'). The RFC identifies future improvements, such as dynamic negotiation of mesh attributes at adjacency startup, dynamic election of transit links, and reduction of CSNP flooding, but notes these are outside the current document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This optimization works, but only if the network is set up correctly. If there's a mistake or a cable breaks unexpectedly, packets might not reach all the routers. In real networks, people usually use a simpler version of this idea rather than the full complex solution.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 2973 is an Informational document that documents existing practice in deployed implementations. It has not been updated or obsoleted. The mechanism it describes is supported by IS-IS implementations and deployed in production networks where mesh topology optimization is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: This document explains a real technique that networks use, and it has not been changed or replaced.
